content.text:
Packing Always Falls to the Parents

Every time you head out, it's always the parents packing the water bottle, snacks, and spare clothes. The child runs out the door in excitement, and you're left scrambling behind to grab whatever was forgotten—always in a rush.

But you can't keep packing for them forever. If a child never learns to get ready on their own, they won't know what to do when something important is missing. Getting ready is an essential life skill a child needs to master.

Curious about the story of the self-reliant child? Let's look at the lesson of the self-reliant child through the illustrations. Meet the key scenes of the self-reliant child's story too. We've gathered all kinds of stories about "12. One, Two, All Set!"—toddler independence stories, picnic preparation stories, building responsibility, and more.
content.caption: Packing easily becomes the parents' job.

content.alt: 12. One, Two, All Set! - Why Getting Ready on Your Own Matters
content.text:
Why Getting Ready on Your Own Matters

The habit of getting ready on your own builds independence and responsibility in a child. By thinking ahead about what's needed and packing it so nothing is left behind, a child learns the power of planning.

What matters is not telling a child what to pack, but helping them realize for themselves why each thing is needed. When a child pictures the outcome—"If I don't have my water bottle, I'll get thirsty"—getting ready becomes their own job rather than something forced on them.
content.caption: When they realize why it's needed, getting ready becomes fun.

content.alt: 12. One, Two, All Set! - Hori's Picnic Packing Story
content.text:
Hori's Picnic Packing Story

In "One, Two, All Set!" Hori is so excited about the picnic that he tries to leave with an empty bag. But when Dad gives the bag a shake, it goes thud—hollow! "What if you get thirsty and there's no water bottle?" At Dad's question, Hori pictures a picnic spot where his throat is bone dry.

Dad lines up the water bottle, snacks, and hat, and they count together. One, water bottle! Two, snacks! Three, hat! As they count and tuck each one in, the bag grows nice and plump. On the next picnic day, Hori packs everything himself, all set before Dad even says a word.
content.caption: Counting them in one by one means nothing gets left behind.

content.alt: 12. One, Two, All Set! - Let's Practice Together at Home
content.text:
Let's Practice Together at Home

After reading, connect the story to real preparations for going out. First, rather than telling them what to pack, let them imagine the outcome: "What would happen if we didn't have a water bottle?"

Second, keep it simple by choosing about three things to pack and let them count and tuck each one in on their fingers. Third, on days they pack by themselves, praise them specifically—"You didn't forget a single thing!"—so they feel the pride of getting ready.
content.caption: On days they pack by themselves, praise them specifically.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions

Q. How can I get my child to prepare on their own?

A. Count out what to pack together—one, two—as you head out and set the order together. Handing off small tasks first helps a child become self-reliant, feeling a sense of accomplishment that builds confidence.

Q. My child keeps forgetting to pack things.

A. Post a picture of what to pack next to the bag, or turn it into a song and check it together. When they finish on their own—"One, two, all set!"—praise them, and it becomes a habit.

Q. Every morning turns into a struggle because getting ready takes so long.

A. Packing together the night before makes mornings far more relaxed. Rather than rushing them, give them time to get ready on their own and celebrate when they do it well.
